title: Some infinities are provably bigger than others
body: Two sets are the same size if their members can be paired off one-to-one. By that test, the counting numbers and the even numbers are equally infinite, even though one seems to contain the other. But Georg Cantor proved that the real numbers can’t be paired with the counting numbers: any attempted list misses some. So the infinity of points on a line is strictly larger than the infinity of 1, 2, 3 and so on.

slides.heading: Make a list
slides.text: Suppose someone claims to have listed every real number between 0 and 1 as an infinite decimal: a first number, a second, a third, and so on forever.

slides.heading: Walk down the diagonal
slides.text: Build a new number whose 1st digit differs from the 1st number’s 1st digit, its 2nd from the 2nd number’s 2nd, and so on, avoiding 0s and 9s.

slides.heading: It can’t be on the list
slides.text: The new number differs from every listed number in at least one place, so the list was incomplete. That holds for any list anyone could make.

slides.heading: Cantor’s diagonal argument in four moves

steps.label: Suppose every real in (0, 1) is on a list
Read off the diagonal: digit n of number n
It differs from every entry: no list works

slides.heading: An endless ladder
slides.text: Cantor also showed that the set of all subsets of any set is always bigger than the set itself, so there is no largest infinity.

slides.question: Why can’t Cantor’s diagonal number be anywhere on the list?
options: It differs from every entry somewhere
It is bigger than every number listed
slides.explanation: Its nth digit was chosen to differ from the nth digit of the nth number, so it differs from every listed number in at least one place. The list was incomplete.

slides.heading: Countable or uncountable?

items.text: All subsets of the counting numbers

slides.explanation: Evens, negatives and even all fractions can be paired off with 1, 2, 3… Cantor showed that the reals, and the set of all subsets of any infinite set, cannot.
